title: One in Four UK Consumers Now Trusts ChatGPT for Financial Advice — and Regulators Are Scrambling
excerpt: As AI chatbots reshape how people manage money, the Mills Review warns of a growing gap between what consumers expect and what the law protects them against.
body:
• More than 25% of UK consumers now trust ChatGPT for financial advice, according to the UK Financial Conduct Authority's Mills Review
  • No AI chatbot is licensed as a financial advisor in any major jurisdiction, creating a growing gap between usage and regulation
  • The EU's AI Act transparency requirements took effect August 2, 2026, requiring AI systems providing financial guidance to disclose they are not human
  • US regulators at the SEC and FINRA have flagged AI-driven financial advice as a 2026 examination priority

The Trust Gap No One Planned For

More than one in four consumers in the United Kingdom now trust ChatGPT to give them financial advice, according to the Mills Review — a landmark assessment of AI in financial services commissioned by the UK's Financial Conduct Authority. The finding captures a shift that has happened faster than anyone in financial regulation anticipated.

The problem is straightforward: no AI chatbot is licensed as a financial advisor anywhere in the world. Not in the UK, not in the US, not in the EU. The models are not designed to give personalized financial advice, their makers explicitly disclaim that purpose, and there is no regulatory framework that holds them accountable when their outputs lead to financial harm.

Yet millions of people are treating them exactly like advisors — asking ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude about portfolio allocation, tax strategies, retirement planning, and individual stock picks. The gap between what these tools are and what consumers use them for is widening every month.

What the Mills Review Found

The Mills Review, published in July 2026, is the most comprehensive assessment to date of how AI is reshaping consumer financial behavior. Beyond the headline trust figure, the review found that younger consumers are significantly more likely to rely on AI for financial decisions, with adoption rates above 40% among 18-34 year olds.

"Nobody licensed AI to give financial advice. But millions of consumers are treating it as though someone did."

— PYMNTS analysis of the Mills Review

The review also identified a troubling pattern: consumers who use AI chatbots for financial guidance tend to have higher confidence in their decisions but no better outcomes than those who don't. In some cases, AI-guided decisions performed worse than simple index fund strategies — a finding that suggests the fluency and authority of chatbot responses may be creating false confidence.

Regulators on Both Sides of the Atlantic

The regulatory response is fragmented and playing catch-up. In the EU, the AI Act's transparency requirements took effect on August 2, 2026, mandating that AI systems providing financial guidance must clearly disclose that they are not human and that their outputs do not constitute licensed financial advice. The provision is a first step, but enforcement mechanisms remain vague.

In the United States, both the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority have flagged AI-driven financial advice as a 2026 examination priority. The SEC's annual exam priorities letter specifically cited "AI and emerging technology use in investment advisory and broker-dealer operations" as an area of heightened scrutiny.

But examination priorities and actual enforcement are different things. As of mid-2026, no US regulator has taken action against an AI company for providing unlicensed financial advice — in part because the existing regulatory framework was built around human advisors and registered firms, not software that generates text.

The NRI Dimension

For Indian-American professionals managing money across two countries — balancing US brokerage accounts, Indian mutual funds, NRE/NRO deposits, and cross-border tax obligations — the appeal of AI-powered financial guidance is obvious. The complexity of NRI financial planning is exactly the kind of problem that chatbots seem well-suited to simplify.

But that complexity is also what makes chatbot advice most dangerous. Cross-border tax law, FEMA compliance, DTAA treaties, and the interaction between US and Indian capital gains rules are areas where a confident-sounding but wrong answer can cost thousands of dollars. No chatbot currently accounts for the specific regulatory environment NRI investors operate in.

Where This Goes

The Mills Review recommends that the FCA develop a new regulatory category for AI-assisted financial guidance — something between unregulated general information and fully regulated personal advice. Whether other regulators follow that lead will shape how hundreds of millions of people interact with their money in the coming years.

For now, the uncomfortable reality is this: the world's most popular AI models are already financial advisors. They just don't have the license, the liability, or the guardrails that come with the title.
